$comment: Declarative readiness evidence for the Manna progress report.
Why a hand-maintained file rather than inference: the statuses below are
CLAIMS, and a claim needs named evidence and a reviewer. Deriving them
automatically would mean guessing — and a dashboard that guesses
'VERIFIED' is worse than no dashboard, because it manufactures exactly
the false confidence the audit record exists to prevent.
So every entry carries an `evidence` string, and changing a status is a
reviewable diff in a pull request. Anything not actually checked is
NOT RUN or BLOCKED, never VERIFIED.
Permitted status values: VERIFIED, PARTIAL, BLOCKED, NOT RUN,
NOT APPLICABLE. No percentages — there is no defined denominator, so a
verifiedAgainstCommit: master at 403acf1, deployed to Vercel Production and CONFIRMED serving (deployment 7344985889 state success; owner-reported dpl_BZgDHuZxjbG2NHgg12b218eoQT3q READY on alias carloscab74.vercel.app). Sprint 1's six PRs: #69 1bc81df, #68 ce7255a, #67 a08c82f, #71 0b609f4, #70 e0f3f0d, #72 403acf1. Suite 61 files / 907 tests passing at e0f3f0d; #72 changed no source file. All four required checks green and ENFORCED by ruleset 25851827. Rows describe master unless one names a PR.

operational.name: Database backup and restore verification
operational.evidence: PROCEDURE VERIFIED SYNTHETICALLY, PRODUCTION REHEARSAL NOT RUN (PR #70). The Phase 0 runbook was executed end to end against a synthetic production-shaped database on 2026-10-25: pg_dump/pg_restore exit 0 with zero stderr in 0.20s; verify-migrate.sql zero non-OK rows; source and target row counts identical; reconciliation-check.sql 7/7 PASS non-vacuously; the application suite passed against the restored database; teardown left nothing behind. Negative cases confirm the checks can fail: a dropped column is caught by step 2, unequal payment legs fail 3 of 7 reconciliation checks, and the privilege probe reports 114 unreachable objects with no grants and 0 with the full set. Evidence: docs/audits/2026-10-25-restore-rehearsal-synthetic.md. What remains NOT RUN is everything production-only: backup availability, recovery point, real restore duration (0.20s on a trivial dataset is not transferable), and production ownership and privileges. Phase 0 is NOT complete.

operational.name: Redis-backed rate limiting in production
operational.evidence: CONFIGURATION CONFIRMED, OPERATION NOT VERIFIED. The owner reports REDIS_URL is set for production (2026-10-20, name only; no value requested or held by this session). That is not the same claim as "limits are shared": lib/rate-limit.ts falls back to in-process counters on any Redis client or command failure. The RAW EXCEPTION is deliberately not logged because it can embed the credential-bearing URL; a degradation line naming the stage and a cumulative count is emitted to stderr, so a signal exists but carries no connection detail. The degradation itself IS caller-visible — allowed and remaining change, and a caller spreading requests across instances can exceed the nominal limit; what is missing is an explicit backend-failure signal. A failure no longer latches: it sets redisDownUntil, which suppresses Redis attempts for a 30s cooldown and then retries, so an instance recovers on its own instead of counting in-process until it recycles. rateLimitBackendHealth() reports activeBackend, cooldown state and the cumulative degradation count, with no credential in it. (An earlier version of this row described the old permanent redisUnavailable latch; that variable no longer exists.) Operational proof needs POST /api/admin/operations/redis-rate-limit run against production with an authenticated admin session holding the exceptions:manage permission — SuperAdmin or OperationsAdmin; a lesser admin role gets 403, which is easy to misread as Redis being down. That route performs an isolated set/get/delete and is already implemented and audited. ONE POST PROVES ONLY THE INSTANCE THAT SERVED IT: the backend state and the in-process counters are module-level in lib/rate-limit.ts, therefore per serverless instance, so another live instance can still be counting in-process while this one answers pass. Serverless instances cannot be addressed individually, so repeated POSTs give sampling confidence rather than coverage; VERIFIED requires evidence covering every live instance, or equivalent deployment-wide evidence, which in practice means monitoring the degradation signal rather than an operator running the route by hand. Nothing external scrapes that signal yet. Row therefore stays PARTIAL on a passing POST. POLICY NOW DECIDED (2026-10-26): the owner ACCEPTED keeping all three money buckets fail-open on Redis loss (docs/decisions/0007, status Accepted), with a fail-closed requirement in the other direction — if velocity_checks cannot be evaluated atomically, the money path must refuse. That holds today only incidentally (checkVelocityLimit has no try/catch and no caller wraps it, so a DB error 500s before any balance moves), with no explicit branch and no test pinning it. A Vercel execution ceiling is now documented — Pro plan, Fluid Compute, 30,000 concurrent executions, 1,000 per 10s per region burst — so 'formally unbounded' is withdrawn at that layer, but it is an EXECUTION ceiling and not an instance count, so no exact in-process multiplier may be claimed. Do not write 30,000 and do not write 'small'.

operational.name: Durable volume control on every money path
operational.evidence: GAP MEASURED 2026-10-26 at 403acf1, and it falsifies a premise of the ACCEPTED decision 0007. That record states velocity_checks is 'the control that actually caps how much a user can move during an outage' for all three money buckets. lib/splits.ts contains ZERO velocity references: paySplitPortion() debits the payer and credits the split creator calling neither checkVelocityLimit() nor recordVelocity(). Because checkVelocityLimit() sums from velocity_checks and split-pay never writes that table, split-pay volume is outside the control in both directions — ungated, and invisible to every other path's velocity budget. Measured per path: send yes/yes, accept-request yes/yes, transfer-intent yes/at-confirm, SPLIT-PAY none/none. So for money:split-pay the Redis-backed 30/hour is the ONLY volume control, degrading to 30/hour x processes on Redis loss with nothing durable behind it. STATED AT ITS REAL SIZE: two structural bounds remain — the debit is conditional (WHERE balance_cad >= amount) so a payer cannot exceed their balance, and a participant can pay only their own portion of a split they belong to, once (ALREADY_PAID). Moving volume this way needs many splits, created through a separate endpoint with its own limit. It is a gap in the decision's stated safety net, not an open drain, and it does NOT flip the decision — the asymmetry that decided it never depended on velocity_checks. BLOCKED on an owner call between two options: add the velocity check and record to the split-pay path so the premise becomes true, or amend 0007 to state that the rate limit is that bucket's only volume control. Neither is implemented, because adding a velocity gate to a money path changes a financial control. Related and also unpinned: the fail-closed-on-velocity-error behaviour 0007 now requires is satisfied only incidentally, by exception propagation, with no test.

operational.name: Branch protection enforcing required checks
operational.evidence: VERIFIED 2026-10-26 by reading the rulesets API. The owner acted on the instructions recorded in the previous version of this row (which read BLOCKED). Ruleset 25851827, "master CI and security checks": enforcement active, target branch, conditions include refs/heads/master with no excludes, bypass_actors EMPTY, and one required_status_checks rule with strict_required_status_checks_policy true requiring exactly the four intended contexts — install · typecheck · lint · test · build; dependency audit; secret scan; analyze javascript-typescript. So the checks are enforced AND a PR must be up to date with master before merging. Two deliberate limits on the claim: the ruleset contains ONLY required_status_checks, so there is no required-review rule and no force-push restriction, and a direct push to master that passes CI is not blocked by it; and the CLASSIC protection API still answers 403 to this environment, so a protected:false reading taken from that endpoint reflects this session's token rather than the absence of protection — the ruleset is the authority. All five Sprint 1 PRs were merged through these required checks.

ownerActions.action: Compare two production requests to settle header trust
ownerActions.why: Send TWO production requests and report, for each, clientIdentity().source AND whether the resolved id EQUALS the forged value that request supplied — a boolean, never the id and never the IP. Request A sends no IP headers. Request B supplies a distinctive forged value in x-real-ip, x-forwarded-for and x-vercel-forwarded-for. The source name alone does NOT answer this: if both requests select x-vercel-forwarded-for the name is identical whether the platform overwrote the forged value or passed it through, so only the equality tells you which happened. If B's id equals what B sent, the header is attacker-controlled and every limit keyed on it is per-attempt, not per-client. PR #71 documents the question; this environment cannot answer it (403 CONNECT to both api.vercel.com and the deployment host).

ownerActions.action: Choose how to close the split-pay volume-control gap
ownerActions.why: Decision 0007 is accepted, but one of its premises is false for one bucket: lib/splits.ts has ZERO velocity references, so paySplitPortion() moves money with neither checkVelocityLimit() nor recordVelocity(). money:split-pay therefore has no durable volume control behind its rate limit, and its volume never consumes any other path's velocity budget. Bounded by the conditional debit and by one-portion-once, so it is a gap in the stated safety net rather than an open drain. Two options, and this is your call because either changes or restates a financial control: (A) add the velocity check and record to the split-pay path, making 0007's premise true — I can implement and test this behind review; or (B) amend 0007 to state that the rate limit is that bucket's only volume control, accepting it explicitly. Also worth pinning either way: the fail-closed-on-velocity-error behaviour 0007 now requires currently holds only by exception propagation, with no explicit branch and no test.
